title: "From Haar Random States to Quantum Machine Learning"
subtitle: "A hands-on numerical tutorial on randomness, scrambling, and learning in quantum systems"

## Background

A recurring lesson in quantum many-body physics and quantum information is that the
typical behaviour of a complex quantum system is sharply constrained, even when its
microscopic details are not. Averages over the unitary group, known as the Haar measure,
together with the concentration of measure that accompanies them, turn this observation
into quantitative predictions. The same low-order Haar moments then reappear in settings
that look, at first, unrelated.

The apparent thermality of a small subsystem follows from the entanglement of typical
states. The recovery of information from an evaporating black hole is governed by the
same Page-curve estimate of subsystem entropy. The protocols that certify quantum
hardware, including randomized benchmarking, cross-entropy benchmarking and classical
shadows, rest on second moments of the Haar measure. The trainability of variational
quantum circuits, through the barren-plateau phenomenon, is fixed by the same
concentration that renders typical states featureless.

The resemblance is not superficial. In each of these cases the underlying object is the
same low-order average over the unitary group, evaluated in a different physical context.
The technical core is correspondingly compact, consisting of Haar averaging, the
Weingarten calculus and a modest amount of representation theory. This tutorial develops
it once and applies it across each setting, with every step carried out explicitly and
checked numerically.

## What you'll learn

A surprising amount of modern quantum theory comes down to one question. **What
happens when you average over random quantum evolutions?** The answer ties together
several topics that look unrelated at first.

> spectral statistics of chaotic Hamiltonians · the entanglement of a typical
> quantum state · how scrambled information hides and re-emerges · why some
> quantum machine-learning models refuse to train.

This tutorial builds the toolkit once and then follows it across all of them.
By the end you will be able to:

- **average over random unitaries by hand** using the Weingarten calculus, and
 predict second- and fourth-moment quantities (purity, frame potentials,
 gradient variances);
- **read the fingerprints of quantum chaos** in a spectrum, level repulsion,
 the spectral form factor, the random-matrix universality classes;
- **quantify scrambling** with out-of-time-ordered correlators, Krylov
 complexity, and tripartite mutual information;
- **use randomness as a tool**, classical shadows, randomized benchmarking, and
 the Hayden-Preskill recovery protocol;
- **explain barren plateaus** and the expressivity-trainability tension in
 quantum machine learning, from first principles.

## How the tutorial is organized

Seven short parts, each a *concept page* followed by *runnable notebooks*:

| Part | You'll be able to… | Notebooks |
|---|---|---|
| [1 · Mathematical Foundations](chapters/01-foundations.qmd) | Speak the language of channels, Lie algebras, state geometry and measure theory | 14 |
| [2 · Random Matrix Theory](chapters/02-random-matrix-theory.qmd) | Diagnose chaos from a spectrum | 3 |
| [3 · Haar Measure & Weingarten Calculus](chapters/03-haar-weingarten.qmd) | Average over random unitaries and derive the Page formula | 7 |
| [4 · Quantum Dynamics & Chaos](chapters/04-dynamics.qmd) | Measure scrambling in real time | 3 |
| [5 · Designs & Clifford Ensembles](chapters/05-designs.qmd) | Replace Haar randomness with something efficient | 2 |
| [6 · Applications of Scrambling](chapters/06-applications.qmd) | Turn randomness into protocols | 5 |
| [7 · Quantum Machine Learning](chapters/07-qml.qmd) | Understand trainability through the same lens | 7 |

You can work through it in order, or jump to whatever you need, since each notebook
stands on its own. A companion **[Exercises & Solutions PDF](exercises.qmd)** collects
analytical problems, worked solutions, and flashcards for every part.

## One calculation across the chapters

These topics are usually learned separately, from different courses and papers, which
hides how closely they are tied. The same Haar average keeps coming back. The second
moment of a random unitary, the twirl that sends an operator to a combination of the
identity and the swap, is computed once in [Part 3](chapters/03-haar-weingarten.qmd) and
then returns as the Page formula, the classical shadows channel, the randomized
benchmarking decay, and the barren-plateau gradient variance. Concentration of measure,
the shrinking of fluctuations as the dimension grows, ties the entanglement of a typical
state to the trainability of a quantum model. Where a notebook reuses an object from an
earlier one, a short Connections note at its end points back to it, so the through-line
stays visible while you work.

## Run it in two minutes

```bash
git clone https://github.com/MarcinPlodzien/quantum-chaos-and-scrambling
cd quantum-chaos-and-scrambling
pip install -r requirements.txt
jupyter lab # open any notebook under source_notebooks/
```

Everything runs on a laptop with a standard scientific-Python stack
(`numpy`, `scipy`, `matplotlib`). No quantum hardware, no GPUs, no special
libraries.

## Who this is for

Graduate students and researchers in quantum information, condensed matter, and
quantum machine learning, and anyone comfortable with linear algebra and Python who
wants to *compute* with these ideas rather than only read about them. It is meant in
particular for people learning these scattered topics on their own, where hands-on,
runnable material is hard to find. The mathematical prerequisites are light and built up
as needed in Part 1.
